title: Problem Details and consistent error contracts
description: Return errors that clients can rely on. Learn RFC 7807 ProblemDetails, envelope patterns, and how to build a consistent error contract across your entire API.

data.text: Error responses are part of your API contract. When every endpoint returns errors in a slightly different shape, clients spend extra code handling exceptions instead of focusing on business logic. A consistent error contract makes your API feel predictable and professional.

This lesson covers the industry-standard RFC 7807 ProblemDetails format, how ASP.NET Core adopts it natively, and how to extend it into a custom envelope that your frontend, mobile apps, and integrations can rely on.

RFC 7807 defines a standard JSON structure for describing errors in HTTP APIs. Instead of inventing a new shape for every endpoint, you return a `ProblemDetails` object that includes a type URI, a title, a status code, a detail string, and an optional instance URI. Clients learn one format and can parse every error the same way.

data.title: Standard ProblemDetails response

data.text: ASP.NET Core 8+ returns `ProblemDetails` automatically for 400 and 500 responses when you call `AddProblemDetails()`. You do not need to manually construct error objects for validation failures or unhandled exceptions.

data.title: Enabling ProblemDetails in Program.cs

data.text: While `ProblemDetails` is excellent for HTTP semantics, many teams prefer an application-level envelope that adds a correlation ID, timestamp, and a machine-readable error code. This envelope is what your frontend and mobile apps actually consume.

data.title: Custom error envelope

data.text: A global exception filter or middleware transforms any exception into this envelope. The client always receives `200` for the envelope structure plus the real status in the body, or you can let the status code pass through and wrap only the body.

Model validation failures are the most common error type. Normalize them into the same envelope your exceptions use. Flatten the `ModelState` dictionary into the `Errors` property so clients receive a predictable structure whether the error came from validation, a business rule, or a database failure.

data.title: Normalizing ModelState into the envelope

data.text: Error codes clients can rely on

Status codes are coarse. Two different validation failures can both return 400, but the client may need to distinguish them. Add a stable, machine-readable `code` field to your envelope—for example, `VALIDATION_FAILED`, `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`, or `PAYMENT_DECLINED`. Codes should never change once published; treat them like a public API.

data.title: Consistency rule
data.text: Every error in your API should follow the same envelope shape. If one endpoint returns `{ message: string }` and another returns `{ errors: [...] }`, client code becomes fragile and hard to test.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Use RFC 7807 ProblemDetails as the HTTP-level standard and extend it for your application.
Normalize all errors—validation, business rules, exceptions—into one envelope shape.
Add stable error codes so clients can react programmatically without parsing human text.
Include a correlation ID and timestamp on every error for support and debugging.
